Please take your seats. Good afternoon. I call to order the informal meeting to conduct an interactive dialogue with Ms. María Fernanda Espinosa, candidate for the position of the United Nations Secretary-General. Today's interactive dialogue marks a critical step in the selection and appointment process for the next Secretary-General, while also coming at a pivotal moment for the United Nations. The person we select will be more than the face of this institution. Our choice will send a powerful message about who we are and whether we truly serve all 8 billion people of the world in all their diversity. The multilateral system, with the United Nations at its centre, is under unprecedented political and financial pressure. From a deepening liquidity crisis to fundamental principles of the UN Charter being put into question, the next Secretary-General will be entrusted not only with navigating these challenges, but also with advancing essential reforms to ensure the United Nations is fit for the future. At the same time, the world needs the United Nations more than ever, and it needs a Secretary-General who can provide strong, principled, and effective leadership across all three pillars: peace and security, sustainable development, and human rights. These interactive dialogues, which I convene in line with General Assembly Resolution 79, Strokes 327, offer unique opportunity for candidates to present their vision for the future of this organization and for member states and civil society to ask questions and interact directly with candidates. The interactive dialogues are essential to ensuring a transparent and inclusive selection appointment process while underlining the important role of the General Assembly. I encourage you to make full use of this opportunity, and I thank all candidates for their active participation, member states and civil society for their questions and engagement. But these dialogues do not end in this chamber. They are also an opportunity for people around the world, the very people the United Nations serves, to listen, to engage, and to hold this process to the highest standards. For this decision does not only concern a few, but all of us in and outside the United Nations who look to this institution to reflect the principles and values it champions. As reflected in my letters dated March 4th, April 15th, and June 1st, 2026, the dialogue will begin with an introduction by the candidate of their vision and priorities, for up to 10 minutes, followed by an interactive exchange. Each interactive dialogue will last up to 3 hours. The interactive exchange will take place in 2 segments. We will begin with a 1.5-hour discussion focused on leadership abilities, experience, and skills needed to lead a strong organization that is fit for the future. Following this, we will move into the second segment, which will focus on the three pillars of the United Nations: peace and security, sustainable development, and human rights. In line with revitalization resolutions, civil society representatives will be invited to pose questions in each of the two thematic segments. Before proceeding to hear the presentation of the vision of the candidate, I would like to inform members on how to inscribe to speak to speak in the two thematic segments. Delegations wishing to speak can register their wish to speak by pressing the microphone button. Please do not press the microphone button yet. I will announce when delegations will be asked to press the microphone button at the beginning of the first segment. Member States speaking on behalf of groups are invited to approach the list of speakers table and will be given priority. Delegations can speak only once in each segment, whether on behalf of a group or in national capacity. In the second segment, priority will be given to delegations that did not have an opportunity to speak during the first segment. By this, I ask the last people entering the room to please take your seat, and I invite Ms. Espinoza to present her vision. Please, you have the floor.

Thank you, thank you, Madam President.

Excellencies, good afternoon. It's an honor to be back here at what has been my home for such a long part of my life as a permanent representative, as Minister for Foreign Affairs, and as President of the General Assembly. This is the feeling that the 8 billion people that you represent should have, that the United Nations are their home, that they belong to all of us. So that's why I would like to speak frankly today, because our people feel the gaps between the promises that we make and and the needs of their daily life.

As Foreign Minister of Ecuador, I hosted talks between the Colombian government and the ELN. I am also a poet, so I know words matter. They have consequences. They can provide hope. We, the peoples, But without action, words are empty. This room, the Trusteeship Council Chamber, is a powerful reminder of what we can achieve when we unite around a common purpose: supporting Member States on their path to peace, to sovereignty and dignity, rebuilding lives, economies and dreams. The purposes and principles of the Charter are as relevant today as they were in 1945, perhaps even more so in this age of complexity. When hard-won progress is under threat, when our systems seem past their prime, when new challenges risk undermining cooperation, when the need has never been greater. That is why we need a UN that everyone can count on. Because no nation is immune to geopolitics and geoeconomics. No nation should bear the burden of acting alone. No nation should be excluded from the benefits that will emerge if and only if we work together. The need for the UN remains undeniable. Yet too often the UN is missing in action or relegated to the sidelines. Too often it is slow, fragmented, and constrained. Financial pressures are not the cause. They are the consequence of deeper challenges. The UN needs to rebuild credibility and show, not just say, that it can deliver real change, be a trusted partner, and add value. I have worked across the UN's pillars and regions. I know the organization inside out, but have never been part of the UN system. I understand its strengths, constraints, and dynamics. I understand its critics. Even them believe in its huge potential. It is up to us to work together to prove the organization's value. I have presided over the most representative body in the world, this Assembly. I come from the ranks of Member States. I have the vision, the stamina, the conviction to serve you all with impartiality and impact. Excellencies, we cannot carry on like this. We must seize this opportunity to build a more effective and trusted UN. Too often we spend our time diagnosing the problems instead of forging solutions. I am deeply honored to be supported by Antigua and Barbuda. Like so many small states, including my own, Ecuador, they have made an outstanding contribution to the UN. A Secretary-General needs to lead as well as listen. That is why, before deciding to pursue my candidacy, I listened to many of you. In after listening, my vision centers on 4 key transformations with proposals that are ready for implementation with member states' blessing, of course. First, we must act early before crisis erupts and the space for diplomacy closes. We must recenter prevention, mediation, and early action as our primary aim. We must make peace possible again. I will establish a prevention and early action hub in my office to ensure that early warnings lead to timely responses. I will work with the Security Council, the primary UN body tasked with the maintenance of peace and security. The Secretary-General and her good offices must be ready to go when and where you need. And I will ensure the UN anticipates and actively manages the global fallout from conflicts, from humanitarian diplomacy, terrorism, and organized crime, to energy shocks, food insecurity, and inflation. This cannot be an afterthought. It must be embedded into our response. Second, we must deliver. The Sustainable Development Goals reflect our shared ambition. But ambition does not feed our children. It does not address debt payments and lack of concessional finance. It does not protect small islands from rising sea levels or reduce trade costs for landlocked developing countries. As Secretary-General, I will work with Member States to assess where progress remains possible drawing on the UN's analytical capacities and deploying AI tools alongside the deep experience of our staff. I will champion fiscal space for national governments. The UN is not the main forum for finance, debt, or trade, but it can be better at convening and as a supporting actor. I will connect the dots between different groups and meetings, reflect the views of those not in the room, and work with all governments, north and south, east and west, to find ways to move forward. I will also consult Member States on a new development approach, one that strengthens national sovereignty while rationalizing the UN's budget and bureaucracy. Development cannot be designed in New York. It must be demand-driven and nationally led. Instead of looking for funds to sustain large programs, we need to focus on a managed transition to a leaner UN that supports national actors. Third, we must leverage our convening superpower. Energy, technology, and demographic changes are reshaping our world at extraordinary pace. The UN is the only forum where all countries can come together to discuss the risks and the opportunities. I will work tirelessly to use the convening power of the UN and of the Secretary-General. On energy, for example, energy issues are fragmented across the UN. I will improve energy security coordination within the UN system to support Member States in addressing shocks and supply chain disruption. On technology, we should build on the Digital Compact and global dialogue on AI. The world benefits most when AI advances responsibly and fosters prosperity. The UN must support AI for the future, not the few. Fourth, we must prove our value every day. The United Nations must be judged by how many lives it saves, and improves. Every reform effort, management decision, and budget discussion must be in service of peace, development, and human rights. If not, we must be brave enough to stop and change course. That will be my guiding principle, building, of course, on the UN Haiti process. Excellent.

Excellencies, in these complex times, we must move beyond binary thinking—secretary or general. As chief administrative officer, I will strive to build a united organization, not a collection of entities competing for resources. I remain a global ambassador, facilitator, and impartial intermediary. I will serve all member states without discrimination. The Secretary-General must never become the representative of a bloc, a region, or any geopolitical alignment. As a peacebuilder, I will place prevention at the heart of my efforts and will strive to preserve political space for dialogue, to strengthen mediation, to support peace initiatives and blue helmets, and to ensure that the organization acts before crises escalate into conflicts and conflicts into catastrophes.

On this constrained geopolitical and financial environment, our choices can feel zero-sum. Sovereignty or cooperation. Principles or pragmatism, cutting costs or saving lives. We must not give into cynicism. International law upholds sovereignty, human rights support peace, educating girls boosts development. There are still win-wins. We can shrink the UN responsibly while strengthening national ownership and delivery and restoring faith in the UN and, of course, in a better future. Excellencies, on this day, 15 June, the Magna Carta was sealed by England's King John. Pioneering French painter Charles de La Fosse was born. Russia made history with its Venus space probe. Benjamin Franklin's scientific discovery changed the course of the world. The Shanghai Cooperation Organization was established. And importantly, the G77 was formed. Every country brings their proud history to the United Nations. That is our strength. No Secretary-General succeeds alone. The future of the UN depends on the collective commitment of member states and the dedication of its staff. I am under no illusion about the difficulties ahead. Yet, I remain optimistic because I have seen what this organization can achieve and the hope it continues to inspire. Muchas gracias.

Thank you very much, and I look forward to continuing the conversation with you.
